lead: An external tester drives every input and reads every output, and it costs money for every second it runs. Built-in self-test (BIST) moves the pattern generator and the response checker onto the chip. An on-chip LFSR makes pseudo-random vectors, a MISR squeezes the responses into a short signature, and one comparison with a stored good signature gives a single pass or fail bit. The chip can then test itself at power-on, after packaging or in the field, with almost no tester.
prereq: You need: shift registers and XOR gates, and scan chains from 6.4.

sections.h3: The BIST loop and its parts

blocks.text: BIST wraps three blocks around the circuit under test (CUT). The test pattern generator (TPG) makes the input vectors. The output response analyser (ORA) compresses the CUT outputs into a short signature. The BIST controller runs the sequence: reset, load the seed, apply the vectors, stop, compare the signature with the good one, set pass or fail.

items: TPG: an LFSR, a binary counter, or a small ROM holding ATPG vectors.
CUT: combinational logic, logic reached through scan chains, or a memory array.
ORA: a MISR, or a simple ones-counter or transition counter; a pass/fail flip-flop holds the result for the tester.

blocks.text: Vectors reach the CUT in two ways. In test-per-clock BIST the TPG drives the CUT inputs directly, one new vector every clock. In test-per-scan BIST the TPG drives the scan-in of each chain and the scan-outs feed the ORA, so each vector needs L shift clocks and one capture clock:

blocks.where: where T is the BIST time in clocks, N the number of vectors, L the length of the longest scan chain, and the 1 the capture clock.

blocks.text: A linear feedback shift register (LFSR) is a shift register whose input is the XOR of a few chosen stages, the taps. With taps taken from a primitive polynomial, an n-stage LFSR steps through every non-zero n-bit word once before repeating; it is then maximal-length.

blocks.where: where n is the number of stages. The one word left out is all zeros.

blocks.text: The all-zero word is a lock-up state: XOR of zeros is zero, so the register would stay there for ever. The seed, the starting word, must be non-zero; different seeds start the same cycle at different points. In the external-XOR (Fibonacci) form the XOR gates combine the taps and feed the first stage; in the internal-XOR (Galois) form one XOR sits between stages, so the feedback passes through only one gate and the register runs faster.

Some faults need a vector a plain LFSR rarely makes; they are called random-pattern-resistant. A 10-input AND gate output stuck-at-0 needs all ten inputs at 1, a chance of 1 in 1024 per vector. A weighted generator ORs two LFSR bits to make a 1 three times in four, or ANDs them to make a 0 three times in four; reseeding loads seeds that expand into chosen ATPG vectors; a test point can also be added to the logic.

A multiple-input signature register (MISR) is an LFSR with one extra XOR in front of each stage, where one CUT output enters each clock. After the last vector the register holds an n-bit signature. It is compared with the golden signature, found by simulating the fault-free design with the same seed and the same vectors.

blocks.where: where P(aliasing) is the chance that a faulty CUT still ends with the golden signature and n is the MISR width. A 16-bit MISR gives about 1 in 65,536.

blocks.text: BIST comes in flavours by its TPG: exhaustive (a counter applies all 2ᵐ vectors to an m-input block), pseudo-exhaustive (each output cone gets all combinations of its own inputs), pseudo-random (the LFSR stream) and deterministic (stored or reseeded ATPG vectors).

A BILBO, built-in logic block observer, is one register with four modes set by two control bits B1 B2: 11 normal register, 00 scan shift register, 10 LFSR or MISR, 01 reset. Between two blocks, the same BILBO is the ORA for the block before it and the TPG for the block after it. The price of BIST is area for the generator, analyser and controller, a little delay on functional paths, and a golden signature that must be re-simulated whenever the netlist changes.

spec.aria: Four flip-flops b3 to b0 holding 0001 with an XOR of b3 and b0 feeding b0, above a ring of the 15 states from 0001 to 1000.

examples.question: A 4-bit LFSR shifts left every clock. Its feedback f = b<sub>3</sub> ⊕ b<sub>0</sub> enters at b<sub>0</sub>, where b<sub>3</sub> is the leftmost bit. Seed it with 0001, list the states until it repeats, and give the period.
steps: Write the state as b<sub>3</sub>b<sub>2</sub>b<sub>1</sub>b<sub>0</sub>. The next state is b<sub>2</sub>b<sub>1</sub>b<sub>0</sub>f.
Fifteen distinct states appear, and 2⁴ − 1 = 15, so every non-zero word appears once: the LFSR is maximal-length.
examples.answer: The period is 15 = 2⁴ − 1, so this LFSR is maximal-length; only 0000 never appears.

examples.question: A 3-bit MISR with state b<sub>2</sub>b<sub>1</sub>b<sub>0</sub> updates as b<sub>2</sub>′ = b<sub>1</sub> ⊕ x<sub>2</sub>, b<sub>1</sub>′ = b<sub>0</sub> ⊕ x<sub>1</sub>, b<sub>0</sub>′ = b<sub>2</sub> ⊕ b<sub>0</sub> ⊕ x<sub>0</sub>, where x<sub>2</sub>x<sub>1</sub>x<sub>0</sub> is the CUT output that clock. It starts at 000. (a) The good CUT gives 101, 011, 110, 001. Find the golden signature. (b) A fault turns the second output into 001. Is it caught? (c) A different fault gives 001, 010, 110, 001. What happens?
steps: (a) 000 with 101 → b<sub>2</sub>′ = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1, b<sub>1</sub>′ = 0 ⊕ 0 = 0, b<sub>0</sub>′ = 0 ⊕ 0 ⊕ 1 = 1: state 101. With 011 → 001. With 110 → 101. With 001 → 011. Golden signature 011.
(b) 101, then 001 → 011, then 110 → 001, then 001 → 010. Signature 010 ≠ 011: the fault is caught.
(c) 001 → 001, then 010 → 001, then 110 → 101, then 001 → 011. Signature 011 equals the golden one, although two output bits were wrong.

In (c) the first error entered b<sub>2</sub> and the second error, one clock later, cancelled it in the feedback: this is aliasing. For n = 3, 2⁻³ = 1 in 8 of long random error streams alias; a 16-bit MISR cuts that to about 1 in 65,536.
examples.answer: Golden signature 011. Fault (b) gives 010 and is caught; fault (c) also ends at 011 and escapes by aliasing, which is why practical MISRs are 16 to 32 bits wide.

traps: Counting 2ⁿ states for a maximal-length LFSR. The period is 2ⁿ − 1; the all-zero word never appears.
Seeding with all zeros. The register locks up at 000…0 and makes no vectors.
Reading a BIST pass as proof of a good chip. A faulty circuit can alias to the golden signature.
Expecting a MISR to say which output was wrong. It only compresses; diagnosis needs the raw responses.
Saying BIST makes ATPG unnecessary. Random-pattern-resistant faults still need weighted, reseeded or ATPG vectors, checked by fault simulation.

quiz.a: Test pattern generator, output response analyser, multiple-input signature register.

quiz.q: What is the period of a maximal-length n-stage LFSR?
quiz.a: 2ⁿ − 1 clocks; every non-zero n-bit word appears once and the all-zero word never appears.

quiz.q: Why must an LFSR seed be non-zero?
quiz.a: With XOR feedback, all zeros gives a feedback of 0 ⊕ 0 = 0, so the register stays at all zeros and produces no vectors.

quiz.q: Give one difference between the external-XOR and internal-XOR LFSR forms.
quiz.a: External-XOR feeds the XOR of the taps into the first stage, so the feedback passes a chain of XOR gates. Internal-XOR puts one XOR between stages, so the feedback passes one gate and the register can run faster.

quiz.q: A 3-bit LFSR shifts left with f = b<sub>2</sub> ⊕ b<sub>0</sub> entering at b<sub>0</sub>. Start from 001, list the states and give the period.
quiz.a: 001 → 011 → 111 → 110 → 101 → 010 → 100 → 001. Seven states, period 7 = 2³ − 1, so it is maximal-length.

quiz.q: A block is tested by test-per-scan BIST with 5,000 vectors through chains of at most 120 flip-flops, at 100 MHz. How long does BIST take?
quiz.a: T = 5,000 × (120 + 1) = 605,000 clocks. At 10 ns per clock, 6.05 ms.

quiz.q: Estimate the aliasing probability of a 20-bit MISR.
A pipeline has block A, a register, then block B. Explain how a BILBO in place of that register supports testing.
quiz.a: Set the BILBO to 10. To test A, a BILBO before A generates vectors and this BILBO compresses A's outputs as a MISR. To test B, this BILBO runs as an LFSR feeding B while the next BILBO compresses. In mode 11 the same flip-flops are an ordinary pipeline register.

beyond: Not for the exam. Logic BIST ships inside most large SoCs and is run at every power-on in cars, where safety standards ask the chip to check itself in the field. Current work combines LFSR reseeding with compression, and keeps switching low so the chip does not overheat while it tests itself. Search 'logic BIST', 'LFSR reseeding' and 'in-system test'.
